title: Universal localizations invert precisely the degenerate-image edge collection
statement: Use small simplicial sets, quasicategories, equivalence edges and coherent functor categories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and universal localization of [def-coef-universally-localizing-simplicial-map]. Let $f:A\to B$ be a universally localizing simplicial map. Put $W_f=\{w\in A_1\mid f(w)=s_0(b)\text{ for some }b\in B_0\}$. Then, for every quasicategory $\mathcal E$ in a sufficiently large universe, restriction along $f$ induces a coherent functor equivalence from $\operatorname{Fun}(B,\mathcal E)$ onto the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(A,\mathcal E)$ on diagrams carrying all edges of $W_f$ to equivalences. No quasicategory, Kan, finiteness or nonemptiness hypothesis is imposed on $A$ or $B$.

source.place: Corollary 6.3.5.5 (02M2), consequence of Proposition 6.3.5.4 (02M1), with the functor-category characterization in Proposition 6.3.1.13 (01MS). These are Kerodon tags, not Stacks tags; no Stacks tag states this coherent theorem. Read online 2026-10-17; archive WANTED.

proof.text: For every small map $g:T\to B$, put $A_T=T\times_B A$, let $p_T:A_T\to T$ be the projection, and let $W_T$ consist of its edges $(e,a)$ with $e=s_0(t)$ for some vertex $t$ of $T$. We prove that $p_T$ is a localization at $W_T$. For any simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to B$, universal localization supplies a collection $V_\sigma$ at which $p_\sigma:\Delta^n\times_B A\to\Delta^n$ is a localization. The set $V_\sigma$ is chosen once for this simplex and works for every target quasicategory.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, implications (2) to (3) and setup of (3) to (4).

proof.text: The simplicial set $\Delta^n$ is the nerve of the linearly ordered category $[n]$: its simplices are monotone vertex lists. An inner horn specifies its consecutive edges and hence this list, whose faces agree with the horn; thus it fills uniquely. An edge $i\leq j$ can have an inverse edge only if also $j\leq i$, forcing $i=j$, so its equivalence edges are exactly its degenerate edges. Take $\mathcal E=\Delta^n$ and the identity functor in the defining universal property of $p_\sigma$. Its restriction $p_\sigma$ must invert $V_\sigma$. Consequently $V_\sigma\subseteq W_{\Delta^n}$. This includes $n=0$.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, proof (3) to (4), first two sentences; explicit ordered-simplex horn and inverse-edge check.

proof.text: Fix a quasicategory $\mathcal E$ and write $\mathcal L_V,\mathcal L_W$ for the full diagram subcategories on $\Delta^n\times_B A$ inverting $V_\sigma,W_{\Delta^n}$ respectively. The preceding inclusion gives $\mathcal L_W\subseteq\mathcal L_V$. Restriction $R:\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^n,\mathcal E)\to\mathcal L_V$ is an equivalence by the definition, and lands in $\mathcal L_W$ because a simplicial map sends a degenerate edge to a degenerate edge, which has itself as inverse with degenerate triangles. Choose an inverse $H$ and a coherent equivalence $\eta:\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal L_V}\simeq RH$. For $G\in\mathcal L_V$, evaluation of $\eta$ at $G$ is an equivalence edge $\eta_G:G\to RH(G)$ in the full diagram subcategory. For $w:x\to y$ in $W_{\Delta^n}$, the pointwise-equivalence theorem makes its components $\eta_x,\eta_y$ equivalences. The square $\eta_G|_{w\times\Delta^1}$ has a diagonal $d$; its two triangles give $[\eta_y][G(w)]=[d]=[RH(G)(w)][\eta_x]$, hence $[\eta_y][G(w)]=[RH(G)(w)][\eta_x]$ in $h\mathcal E$. The right side and $[\eta_y]$ are invertible, so $[G(w)]$ is invertible. The mapping-composition theorem identifies this with $G(w)$ being an equivalence. Thus every vertex of $\mathcal L_V$ lies in $\mathcal L_W$, and the two full simplicial subsets are equal. This proves the claim for every standard simplex.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, proof (3) to (4), enlargement of the inverted collection; the two inclusions and inverse-square argument explicitly expand Corollary 6.3.1.23 (02LT).

proof.text: Call a simplicial set $T$ good if the claim of step 1 holds for every $g:T\to B$. Every standard simplex is good by steps 1–3, and $\varnothing$ is good because both functor simplicial sets out of $\varnothing$ are the one-point simplicial set. For finite $T$, meaning finitely many nondegenerate simplices, induct on dimension and, in each fixed dimension $n\geq0$, on the number of nondegenerate $n$-simplices. The boundary-cell presentation applied to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow T$ attaches exactly its nondegenerate simplices in increasing dimension; a finite coproduct of attachments can be performed one cell at a time, since both quotients identify exactly the prescribed boundary pairs. Choose the last $n$-cell. It gives a degreewise pushout $T=T^{\prime}\amalg_{\partial\Delta^n}\Delta^n$, where $T^{\prime}$ has fewer $n$-cells and $\partial\Delta^n$ has smaller dimension. For $n=0$, the boundary is empty. Thus $T^{\prime}$ and $\partial\Delta^n$ are good by the induction hypothesis, and $\Delta^n$ is good by the simplex case.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, finite double induction and the cell-attachment pushout; the existing boundary-cell node supplies the simplicial attachment theorem.

proof.text: Fix $g:T\to B$ in this attachment. Pulling back the four corners along $A\to B$ gives another degreewise pushout: in each degree, a pair $(t,a)$ is represented by a representative of $t$ in either summand paired with the same $a$; all representatives and identifications lie over the same element of $B$, so the equivalence relations on pairs are exactly the pulled-back identifications. The maps $\partial\Delta^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ and $A_{\partial\Delta^n}\hookrightarrow A_{\Delta^n}$ are degreewise injective. Every map of the spans preserves the collections $W$, since it preserves $s_0$. Moreover $W_T$ is the union of the two images of $W_{T^{\prime}}$ and $W_{\Delta^n}$: an edge $(s_0t,a)\in W_T$ lifts by choosing a representative vertex $t_i$ of $t$ in either summand and using $(s_0t_i,a)$. The equality $g_i(s_0t_i)=f(a)$ follows from its image in $B$. Conversely every such lifted edge has degenerate $T$-coordinate. This argument does not assume that the attaching simplex is injective or that $T$ reflects degeneracy.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, application of the localization-gluing proposition: explicit pullback pushouts, monomorphisms and union of the vertical edge collections.

proof.text: Apply the localization pushout theorem with source span $A_{\partial\Delta^n}\to A_{\Delta^n},A_{T^{\prime}}$, target span $\partial\Delta^n\to\Delta^n,T^{\prime}$, and edge collections $W_{\partial\Delta^n},W_{\Delta^n},W_{T^{\prime}}$. The three vertical maps are localizations by the simplex case and the induction hypothesis. Step 5 verifies both injective legs, compatibility of edge collections, and the two pushouts. The theorem therefore makes $p_T$ a localization at the union of the two edge images, which is exactly $W_T$. This completes both inductions and proves goodness for all finite $T$.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, proof (4) to (1), the concluding cell-gluing application of Proposition 6.3.5.3.

proof.text: For any small $T$, let $I$ be the poset of its finite simplicial subsets, ordered by inclusion. It is small and nonempty (it contains $\varnothing$); the union of two finite subsets is finite and is a common upper bound. Every simplex is contained in the subset it generates, which is finite: factoring a monotone operator as a surjection followed by an injection shows that every generated simplex is a degeneracy of one of the finitely many faces of the generator. Thus $T=\varinjlim_{S\in I}S$ degreewise. For a fixed $g:T\to B$, also $A_T=\varinjlim_{S\in I}(S\times_B A)$: any pair $(t,a)$ appears as soon as $t$ lies in $S$, and all maps are inclusions. Finally $W_T=\bigcup_{S\in I}\operatorname{im}(W_S)$: for $(s_0t,a)$ choose $S$ containing the vertex $t$. These statements identify the actual diagram of maps and its specified edge collections, not only its underlying objects.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, reduction to finite simplicial sets: explicit finite-subset index, degreewise filtered colimit and marked-edge union.

proof.text: Each map $S\times_B A\to S$ in step 7 is a localization at $W_S$ by the finite case, and all transition maps preserve these collections. The filtered-colimit localization theorem applies to the small nonempty filtered index $I$, giving that $p_T:A_T\to T$ is a localization at $W_T$. Now take $T=B$ and $g=\mathrm{id}_B$. The degreewise isomorphism $A\to B\times_B A$, $a\mapsto(f(a),a)$, identifies $p_T$ with $f$ and identifies $W_T$ with $W_f$. By the definition of localization, this is precisely the asserted equivalence of full coherent functor categories for every $\mathcal E$ in a sufficiently large universe.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.5.4, filtered-colimit reduction via Corollary 6.3.2.12 (05ZQ), then Corollary 6.3.5.5 (02M2), specializing to the identity base change.
